analysis.one_liner: Creates a national charter for nonbank consumer lenders that overrides state interest-rate caps and licensing.
analysis.headline: With 8 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, then a subcommittee, and died without a vote when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let state-licensed nonbank lenders — the companies behind payday, installment, and small-dollar loans — apply for a federal "National Consumer Credit Corporation" charter. With that charter, a lender could operate nationwide under one federal rulebook, and the bill expressly forbids any regulator, federal or state, from capping its interest rates or fees. It pairs this with some borrower safeguards: a $5,000 cap on unsecured loans per borrower, a required ability-to-repay check, a free extended repayment plan once a year, and a true-cost statement in the loan agreement. The bill never received a committee markup or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Nonbank consumer lenders — payday, installment, and small-dollar credit companies — gain the most: a single federal charter lets them lend in every state at whatever rate the market allows, freeing them from state usury caps, licensing regimes, and conflicting rules. Some underbanked consumers gain a new, federally supervised source of small-dollar credit they cannot get from banks, with disclosure and repayment-plan protections attached.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Comptroller of the Currency to charter nondepository creditors that focus primarily on serving underserved consumers and small businesses, giving them a single nationwide operating charter.

Requires lenders to verify a borrower can repay, caps unsecured loans at $5,000 per borrower ($25,000 for secured or small-business loans), bans loans of 30 days or less and prepayment penalties, and requires a free extended repayment plan at least once every 12 months for borrowers who cannot repay short-term loans.

Requires clear disclosure of the true cost of a loan — all interest and fees as a dollar amount and a percentage of principal — plus financial counseling and credit-building information for every borrower offered a product.
Gives state attorneys general power to investigate and sue charter lenders, and gives the Comptroller examination, suspension, and revocation authority over charters.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers — particularly in states that cap interest rates — lose those caps under the bill: it forbids any governmental entity from setting a usury limit on chartered lenders, so loans legal only at high rates in a few states could be marketed everywhere. State governments lose licensing and oversight authority over chartered lenders, and state attorneys general must give the Comptroller advance notice and their complete complaint before suing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Borrowers in rate-cap states and state regulators

drawbacks.text: Section 3(j) forbids the Comptroller and every other government entity from establishing any usury limit or cap on interest, fees, or charges for chartered lenders — the one provision that would let states keep high-cost credit in check is expressly nullified.

Chartered lenders are exempt from state licensing, office-location, education, and training laws, and from any state law that 'prevents or significantly interferes' with their business — stripping state consumer-protection regimes that currently govern these lenders.

A new financial product is automatically deemed approved if the Comptroller does not act within 45 business days, shifting the burden onto regulators to disapprove products after they reach the market.

For loans of one year or less, the bill replaces the standard annual-percentage-rate disclosure with a dollar-amount and percentage-of-principal statement, making side-by-side rate comparison with other credit products harder.
Protections are narrow in scope: the free extended repayment plan is available only once per 12 months, and the statutory penalty for knowing violations is capped at $10,000 per day.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The borrower protections are real but sit alongside the bill's central feature: eliminating state interest-rate caps for chartered lenders. For a borrower in a state that caps rates, losing that cap could outweigh the new disclosures and repayment plans, since the bill defines 'affordable' only as a loan the borrower is expected to be able to repay — not one at a reasonable price. The bill was structured around what the industry needed to operate nationwide, with consumer safeguards attached rather than primary.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, sent down to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer introduced the bill on July 18, 2012, joined by Rep. Joe Baca, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee held hearings on the bill before referral, and the bill was referred to that subcommittee on October 1, 2012.
No further action was taken: the full committee never marked up the bill, no vote occurred in either chamber, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers in states with interest-rate caps kept those protections, state regulators kept their authority over small-dollar lenders, and the nonbank lender industry did not get its federal charter.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever took place, so no roll calls exist; sponsorship was nominally bipartisan — the sponsor was a Republican joined by one Democrat, and 6 of the 8 cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.industry: Nonbank small-dollar lenders (payday, installment, auto title)
industries.note: The bill hands this industry a federal charter to operate in all 50 states and expressly bans any government from capping its rates or fees, overriding the state usury laws that currently limit what it can charge. Its gain comes directly from borrowers who would face rates their states had outlawed.

industries.industry: State governments and state consumer-protection regimes
industries.note: State licensing, office-location, and training rules are preempted for chartered lenders, and state attorneys general must notify the Comptroller and share their complete complaint before suing. States would lose their main tools for policing high-cost credit.

Banks and credit unions may own, affiliate with, or form joint ventures with the new chartered lenders, but the charter also creates new competitors for the small-dollar loan business banks have struggled to serve profitably.
